1:
The opening declaration is read as a rebuke to confidence in the temple. Matthew Henry sets the occasion: the Jews gloried in the temple and promised themselves great things from it, and to shake that confidence both the prophets and Christ foretold its ruin. After the Chaldean destruction it recovered and the ceremonial services revived, but the later destruction made it a perpetual desolation and abolished the ceremonial law with it; and to prepare the world for this they were often told how little account the temple was with God. Henry draws out the argument: if his throne is so bright and his footstool so large, where is the house that can be the residence of his glory? What satisfaction can the Eternal Mind take in a house made with men’s hands, or what occasion has he for a house to repose in, who faints not and is never weary? John Gill takes the heaven named as the highest, where the divine majesty is displayed, so that we are to look upward and not imagine that God dwells in temples made with hands or is confined to any place on earth; he notes that the words were quoted for this purpose by Stephen. John Wesley glosses the clauses the same way.

Charles Ellicott asks what the historical occasion was and leaves it open. Was the prophet condemning in advance the restoration of the temple after the return, or the intention of some exiles to build one in the land of their captivity, as others afterwards did in Egypt? Was he anticipating the vision that in the new Jerusalem there is no temple? Neither view satisfies him, since other passages of the book and three later prophets all presuppose a new temple. It seems better, he concludes, to see the strongest form of the truth that God does not dwell in temples made with hands—compatible, as in Solomon and our Lord and Stephen who quoted this passage, with the profoundest reverence for the visible sanctuary. He adds a parallel a scholar cites from an Egyptian hymn of the fourteenth century before Christ, in which the writer says of God that his abode is not known and no building can contain him. Adam Clarke gives the chapter’s design more polemically, taking the Jewish ritual and people as shadowing forth Christianity and its professors, so that the idolatries of the one stand for those afterwards practised by those bearing the Christian name.

The second verse turns from what God does not need to what he regards. Ellicott traces the sequence: the Maker of the universe can need nothing belonging to it, and the most stately temple is to him as the infinitely little; what he delights in is generically different, the spiritual life answering to his own, the contrite heart which is the true correlative of his holiness. He who offers that is a true worshipper with or without ritual; here, he observes, the two halves of the book are one in teaching. Gill infers from creation that since God made the heavens and the earth he must be omnipresent and cannot be included in any place. Wesley adds that the things were not only made by God but kept in being by him, and glosses the trembling as trembling at God’s threatening words and hearing every revelation of his will with reverence. Keil and Delitzsch supply the link to what follows: so far as the mass of the exiles were concerned, who had not been humbled by their sufferings, God wanted neither temple nor sacrifice; the acts to which such detestable predicates are applied end in the merely external, the offerer’s feelings being opposed to the idea of the sacrifice, so that they are dead works of men spiritually dead. Clarke notes that a word necessary to the sense has dropped from the same verse, preserved by two ancient versions.
3:
The third verse pairs legitimate offerings with atrocities, and the commentators divide sharply over what the pairing means. Charles Ellicott takes it as emphasis by iteration, each clause giving a distinct illustration of the previous verse: an earlier chapter had pointed to tendencies leading to open apostasy, and now the prophet declares that there may be as real an apostasy beneath an orthodox creed and an irreproachable ritual, each act of the hypocrite’s worship being as an idolatrous abomination. John Wesley reads it the same way and insists on the limit: the prophet is not reflecting here on idolatrous worship but on formal worship, on those who in a formality worshipped the true God by acts he had appointed, and God declares that their services were no more acceptable to him than murder or the most horrid profanation of his name. He finds a full commentary on the whole verse in the proverb that the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination, and glosses the closing clauses as meaning that they live as they list and take pleasure in their sins. John Gill gives a different account altogether. The offerer is not blamed because the animal was blemished or the sacrifice irregular, but because all such sacrifices are now abolished, the great sacrifice having been offered; to continue them, as he says the unbelieving Jews did daily until the destruction of the temple, was as grievous to God as murder, being a trampling of the Son of God underfoot and an accounting of his blood as nothing.

Adam Clarke reads the verse as a charge of wickedness joined with hypocrisy—the most flagitious crimes committed by those who at the same time affected great strictness in the external services of religion—and cites a prophet who upbraids the people with slaying their children to idols and then coming the same day into the sanctuary, and the hypocrisy of those who devoured widows’ houses and for a pretence made long prayers. He complains that most interpreters, by departing from the literal rendering, have lost the true sense and substituted what makes no good sense at all, since it is not easy to show how sacrifice and murder, or legal offerings and idolatrous worship, could possibly be of the same account in the sight of God. His own rendering makes the two halves of each clause identify the same act rather than compare two. He also notes that a word necessary to complete the sense is perhaps irrecoverably lost from the second clause, the Latin and Chaldee supplying a verb from necessity rather than from any different reading, since it seems to have been missing before the oldest of them; and he records another scholar’s proposal to repeat a word from the beginning of the member, which he answers by observing that this is not done in the parallel members.

The reply in the fourth verse turns their choice back on them. Ellicott finds in the Hebrew noun the thought of the turnings and windings of fortune, what has been called the irony of history, and says these are the instruments with which God mocks those who mock him by their hypocrisy: their choice did not delight him, and what he chooses will be far other than delightful for them. Wesley states the same reciprocity plainly—they have chosen to delude, and God will choose to let them delude themselves; they have chosen to work wickedness, and he will choose the effect—and glosses their fears as the things which they feared, adding that God accounts those not to hear who do not obey his will. Gill takes the delusions concretely, as God suffering them to choose teachers who would deceive them, wolves in sheep’s clothing who through an appearance of sanctity deceived many, and false Christs whom they embraced after rejecting the true one and by whom they were ruined.
5:
The address turns from the hypocrites to the persecuted, and everyone notices the turn. Matthew Henry says the prophet, having denounced judgments against a hypocritical nation that made a jest of God’s word, now speaks to those who trembled at it, to assure them they shall not be involved in the judgments coming on their nation. Ministers must so distinguish, he adds, that when they speak terror to the wicked they do not make the hearts of the righteous sad; and he puts the principle in a Latin tag, that this is nothing to the good Christian. The word of God has comforts for those whom true humiliation has prepared to receive them—there were those who when God spoke would not hear, but if some will not, others will, and if the heart trembles at the word the ear will be open to it. Charles Ellicott identifies the parties: the self-righteous repudiate and as it were excommunicate the true worshippers, and taunt them with their devotion to a God who does not help them, saying let the Lord glorify himself that we may look on your joy—words which find an echo at the cross. The prophet adds the doom that shall fall on the mockers, that they and not those they deride shall be put to shame. John Wesley reads the brethren as brethren by nation, who cast them out of their synagogues and some out of the world, thinking they did God service. John Gill takes the address as spoken for the comfort of believing Jews.

Henry applies the verse to the first preachers of the gospel rather than to the return from captivity, since nothing like it appears in that history: the apostles were Jews by birth, and their own countrymen were their bitterest enemies even in Gentile cities; their brethren, who should have encouraged them for their work’s sake, cast them out of their synagogues as blemishes when they were really blessings. He hears the same complaint in the Song, and in the reproach with which one governor upbraided Christ, that his own nation had delivered him up. Adam Clarke is occupied with a variant: the Syriac and one edition of the Greek read say ye to your brethren that hate you rather than your brethren that hated you said, a reading two ancient commentators follow; the common Greek text, he notes, is not easy to make sense of.

The sixth verse is heard as a sound before it is understood as a sentence. Keil and Delitzsch render its three clauses as interjectional exclamations—sound of tumult from the city, sound from the temple, sound of the Lord who repays his enemies with punishment—and explain that the third drops the note of exclamation because it approaches a plain statement, the speaker announcing who is the cause of a noise that was at first enigmatic. They add that the city and temple are for these mockers nothing but the places from which judgment will issue; both were still lying in ruins as the prophet spoke, yet both preserve the holiness conferred on them, being where God will take up his abode once more. Ellicott hears the same dramatic effect, the words representing the wonder with which men will behold the great judgments of God proceeding, as with the thunders of Sinai, from the city and the temple that seemed to have been given over to destruction. Gill locates the noise at the taking of Jerusalem, when the shouts of the soldiers and the shrieks of the inhabitants were heard from it, and reports a Jewish commentator who referred it instead to a future conflict. Clarke adds the detail that similar words were spoken by a man of the same name as the prophet’s Lord shortly before the city fell, whose affecting history the historian of that war relates.
7:
The image of a birth without labour is the chapter’s most striking figure, and the commentators agree on the mother and differ on the child. Charles Ellicott identifies both: the mother, as the next verse shows, is Zion, and the man-child born without the travail-pangs of sorrow is the true Israel of God; the figure has appeared twice already in the book, its antithesis being an earlier passage where the children come to the birth and there is no strength to bring forth. Keil and Delitzsch read the boy as a whole land full of men, an entire nation, and describe the seer exclaiming with amazement at a delivery of such rapidity; they note that the verb means to cause to glide out. John Gill takes Zion as a woman who brings forth suddenly and easily, the pangs as soon as they come being gone; and he explains why the passage stands here, lest it be thought that the interest of Christ would be swallowed up in the destruction of the Jews. He refers it to the conversion of many of that people both in the first times of the gospel and in the latter day, together with the calling of the Gentiles and the uniting of both in one church. John Wesley reads the whole verse as expressive of a great and sudden salvation, and refers it to the coming of Christ and the sudden propagation of the gospel.

The questions of the eighth verse are read as wonder rather than doubt. Gill takes them of numerous conversions, unheard of and never before seen in the world, amazing even to the church herself. Ellicott corrects a phrase—shall a land be made to travail rather than shall the earth be made to bring forth—and finds the point in a contrast, the usually slow processes of national development set against the supernatural rapidity of the birth and growth of the new Israel. Wesley makes the same contrast historical, that as soon as the voice of the gospel put the church of the Jews into her travail in the time of Christ and the apostles, it presently brought forth. Adam Clarke reports that a large number of manuscripts, including four ancient ones and the two oldest editions, add a conjunction at the start of the second question, and that all the ancient versions read it so.

The ninth verse answers the wonder with a question of God’s own. Ellicott finds the implied thought to be that God will not leave his work of national restoration unfinished, and that there shall not be that frustration of hopes just when they seem on the point of fulfilment which the history of the world so often records. Wesley expands the argument into two: shall he who gives a birth to women to whom he has given power to conceive not give a birth to his people, whom by his promises he has made to conceive such expectations? and shall Zion bring forth only once? Her womb shall not be shut; she shall every day bring forth more children, and God’s presence shall be with his church to the end of the world. Gill uses the verse to keep the credit where he thinks it belongs: lest too much should seem to be attributed to the church, who is said to travail and bring forth, this is spoken by the Lord—the church may pray and her ministers preach, and both be said to travail, but it is the Lord who brings to the birth, since regeneration is not the work of man but of God. Clarke gives the literal force of the Hebrew phrase, which denotes what immediately precedes the appearance of the child, and adds that it is an expression which should be studiously avoided in prayers and sermons.
10:
The call to rejoice is addressed to those outside the household. Charles Ellicott keeps the figure running: the holy city is still thought of as a mother rejoicing in her new-born child, and friends and neighbours who had shown pity for her sufferings are now invited to share her joy—the nations friendly to Israel being meant. John Gill supplies the domestic comparison, that as when a woman is delivered her friends and neighbours congratulate her and rejoice with her, as happened at the birth of John the Baptist, so the church’s friends are called together to rejoice at the numerous conversion of souls in her, than which nothing is more joyful to the saints.

The eleventh verse turns the guests into nurslings. Ellicott says the figure takes a new and bolder form, the friends who visit the rejoicing mother being invited to take their place with the new-born child and share his nurture; the underlying thought is that the heathen nations friendly to Zion were to become converts and be incorporated with her citizens. Gill weighs the connective. On the received rendering the clause states the purpose for which the church’s friends were called; but he thinks it better rendered either as a consequence, since they mourned with her and rejoiced with her, or, better still, as a reason why they should rejoice—because they partake of her privileges and ordinances. He notes that the singular noun stands for the plural, and identifies the consolations as Christ and his Spirit, Christ being a full breast of comfort in the greatness of his person and the riches of his grace. John Wesley is briefer, taking the gospel doctrine for the breasts of consolation and Christ for the glory named in the second clause, who was the glory of Israel though also a light to the Gentiles.

One word in the same verse is thought corrupt. Adam Clarke reports that two manuscripts and an early edition read a different letter, and that in three others the letter stands on an erasure; he observes that two Jewish commentators, unable to make anything of the word as it stands, say it means the same as the variant—which, he remarks, is in effect to admit a various reading or an error while disguising the admission. He asks what sense there is in sucking nourishment from the splendour of a glory, notes that one commentator tried to deduce another sense of the word without authority so far as he can see, and proposes instead a reading meaning from the stores, from a verb to nourish, found in one manuscript; he thinks one ancient translator may have understood it so, and that two others and the Latin nearly agree.

The twelfth verse gives the reason for all this. Keil and Delitzsch explain that God turns peace to Jerusalem, the greatest of inward blessings, and at the same time the glory of the Gentile world, the most splendid of outward ones, both in the richest superabundance, so that the nurslings may suck and be borne upon arms and fondled upon knees. Clarke identifies the two waters concretely as the great river and the Nile, and holds that two words meaning at the breast have dropped from the text through their likeness to the two words following, a conjecture he calls very probable and which he supports by noting that the Chaldee and Latin omitted the latter pair instead. Gill takes the river as any great flowing stream that brings blessing where it comes, and distinguishes the times: this does not respect the first times of the gospel, since although Christ made peace and preached it and many enjoyed spiritual peace, the churches had very little outward peace and what they had did not last; in the latter day, he says, not only spiritual peace but outward peace in great abundance and lasting continuance will be possessed.
13:
The comparison changes once more, and Charles Ellicott marks the change precisely. The image of maternal love, with which the prophet’s mind is full, is presented in yet another aspect: the love Zion gives and the love her children receive from the nations are both only shadows of the infinite tenderness of God. In this instance the object of the mother’s love is not the child at the breast but the full-grown man, returning like the prodigal to his home after long years of exile; and Ellicott finds the words characteristic both of the special tie that unites son to mother more than to father in most eastern nations and perhaps of the prophet’s own memories. Keil and Delitzsch read the shift the same way, that the prophet now looks on the members of the church as grown from childhood to maturity, so that they suck like a child and are comforted like a grown son. They answer an objection to the word chosen, that a critic thought it ill selected when the writer could easily have written son as he does elsewhere; but he writes man, they say, not in the weak sense the Greek version gave it, but looking on the people whom he had thought of as children as standing before him as one man. Israel is now like a man escaped from bondage and returned home from a foreign land, full of mournful recollections which entirely disappear in the maternal arms of divine love in the beloved home that had been the home of his thoughts even in the strange land. John Gill keeps the agency clear: though ordinances are means and ministers are instruments of comfort, God is the sole efficient cause, and it is wonderful that he should condescend to administer it, being the high and lofty One while those he comforts are dust and ashes who have sinned against him. He lists what nevertheless confirms the promise—an everlasting love that gave his Son and quickened them when dead in sin, a covenant taken with them, and a promise from one who never fails. John Wesley says only that the comfort is given in the most tender and compassionate way.

The fourteenth verse describes the effect of seeing what has been promised. Keil and Delitzsch take the seeing as the enjoyment of a heart-cheering prospect, so that the beholders revive with the smiling scenery around them; they read the body as a tree of which the bones are the branches, which will move and extend in the fulness of rejuvenated strength. So, they say, the hand of God practically makes itself known in his servants—the hand under whose gracious touch all vernal life awakens, whether in body or in mind—while he is fiercely angry with his foes. Ellicott sets out the same figure as a pair of symbols, heart and bones standing for the inner and the outer life, the bones being the branches of the body, which had been dry and sere and should revive as with the sap of a new life and be as succulent herbage; the hand, he adds, is God’s manifested power, shown in love to his people and in indignation to their enemies. Wesley reads the joy as belonging to all who fear God, since the peace of the church and the propagation of Christ’s kingdom is always the cause of a rejoicing heart, so that they flourish like a herb in the spring; and he glosses the hand as the power, protection and influence of God. Gill takes the seeing as the arrival of everything prophesied—the conversion of the Jews and the peaceable condition of the church—perceived and felt and enjoyed in an experimental way.
15:
The chapter turns to judgment. Matthew Henry describes its double aspect: these verses, like the pillar of cloud and fire, have a dark side towards the enemies of God’s kingdom and a bright side towards his faithful subjects. He refers them probably to the Jews in captivity, some sent there for their hurt, others for their good; but the prophecy looks further, to the judgment for which Christ came once and will come again. In the great day, Henry adds, the wrath of God will be his fire and sword, and his word when it takes hold of a conscience burns like fire and is sharper than a two-edged sword. Keil and Delitzsch describe the theophany: God comes in fire, since it is the fiery side of his glory in which he appears, fire being the intense excitement of the powers of destruction within God himself, then transformed into destructive powers in the world; he is compared to a warrior driving war-chariots that resemble stormy wind. They prefer in fire to the Greek version’s as fire. Adam Clarke prefers the Greek, whose translators had the comparative particle in their copy, and proposes a different pointing of another verb so that God breathes forth his anger rather than renders it. Charles Ellicott reads the chariots as storm-clouds sweeping on their way while the lightnings do their work, and John Wesley allows fire in a proper sense, as that with which enemies consume the places they take, adding that fury properly taken is not in God but stands for fervour.

The sixteenth verse states the judgment’s extent. Keil and Delitzsch take the fire as pointing to destructive occurrences of nature and the sword to those of history, while laying all the emphasis on the direct action of God himself. Ellicott prefers hold judgment to plead, and observes that fire and sword, used by the enemies of God against his people, become in turn the instruments of his vengeance, though the sword may equally symbolise divine judgment apart from any human instrument. Wesley notes that God first pleads with sinners by words and, if he cannot so prevail, in a way by which he will overcome. John Gill applies the verse to particular powers of his own reckoning of history, naming the Ottoman empire and the ecclesiastical adversaries he identifies with the figures of the Revelation.

The seventeenth verse describes those judged, and one word in it is the hardest crux. Keil and Delitzsch say the judgment falls not only on the heathen but on the great mass of Israel who had become like them, and note the bigoted thoroughness implied by the pairing of two synonyms for consecrating and purifying; the gardens they take as places of worship. Clarke devotes his note to the phrase behind one tree. The Syrians, he reports, worshipped a god held to be the highest of all and identified with Jupiter and the sun, whose name an ancient writer says signifies one, as the Hebrew word here does; the name appears in a weaker form in two of their royal names, taken from their chief object of worship. The marginal reading, however, gives the feminine form of the same word, which thirty manuscripts and the two oldest editions follow, and a scholar he cites approves it and supposes the moon-goddess to be meant, with arguments Clarke does not think improbable. Two ancient versions and two Greek translators cut through the difficulty by taking the word in its common meaning rather than as a name, giving the sense of one after another; and whatever the particular idolatry, the general sense of the place is clear. Gill takes those who sanctify themselves as pretending to a holiness they do not have, and reports two Jewish commentators who read the word as preparing to worship an idol on an appointed day.
18:
The eighteenth verse opens with a grammatical gap. Charles Ellicott observes that the Hebrew has no verb, either for emphasis, as in a famous broken sentence of Virgil, or through an accidental omission; many supply I know, others I will punish or I have seen. The thought in any case is that the eye of God sees the evil done in the secret places where the heathen rites were celebrated. Adam Clarke holds a word simply lost, supplied from the Syriac, paraphrased by the Chaldee as their deeds are manifest before me, and represented in two editions of the Greek; he thinks it certainly genuine, and proposes a second correction so that the following participle answers to it. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the verse begins with a harsh ellipsis, and record another scholar’s attempt to avoid the difficulty by taking the seventeenth verse of the idolatrous world outside Israel, so that when their thoughts and actions succeed in bringing all nations together against Jerusalem, they come and see the alarming manifestation of God’s power; but this, they object, leaves the opening pronoun without a function. They read the passage as marking out the way Israel’s history will take—the winding but memorable path by which, as the Apostle sets it out, the compassion of God reaches its all-embracing end, with a universal judgment as the turning-point. Ellicott notes that the phrase all nations and tongues, though not incompatible with the prophet’s authorship, is specially characteristic of the prophets of the exile, and takes the glory they are to see as God’s glory manifested in his righteous judgments on open enemies and concealed apostates. John Wesley reads the glory differently, as the oracles and ordinances hitherto locked up in the church of the Jews and now to be published to the Gentiles. John Gill takes the opening words as declaring knowledge and vengeance together, the works and thoughts of those described being known to the discerner of the heart.

The sign and the mission that follow are read variously. Gill canvasses the possibilities for the sign—a miracle, the wonders wrought in the Gentile world, the conversion of the Jews, a distinguishing mark such as was set on Cain—and settles on an ensign set up to gather people, taking it of Christ, a sign spoken against, raised in the ministration of the gospel to gather souls. Ellicott allows that the sign may be one of supernatural terror, but thinks the context makes supernatural deliverance more probable; the thought of a remnant to be saved is still dominant, and that remnant is to act as heralds to the far-distant nations which had taken no part in the open antagonism to Israel. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way, that a remnant escapes and is employed to promote the conversion of the Gentile world.

The nations named are then identified, and the identifications differ. Ellicott takes the first either for Spain or vaguely for the far west; the second stands for a name found in the Greek denoting an African people, and the third, in the judgment of most scholars, not for the Lydians of Asia Minor but for an African nation famous for archery. He records a contrary view, that the second is a people of Italy and the third the Lydian soldiers by whose help an Egyptian king made himself independent. The fourth he refers to the shores of the Black Sea, the fifth to Greek settlements which carried on an active trade with Tyre. Clarke suspects that the words rendered who draw the bow are a corruption of the name of a nation between two seas, properly joined with the name following, and notes that the Greek gives the name without anything about the bow, the participle having been taken for a noun and the bow added to make sense of it; he also prefers my name to my fame.
20:
The return of the exiles is itself the offering. Charles Ellicott presses the word: it is the bloodless meat-offering of the law, and the thought is that the returning exiles would be the most acceptable offering that could be brought to God—an idea found in a later prophet and transferred to Gentile converts by the Apostle. The conveyances point to the habits of the many nations sharing in the work, and the clean vessel is answered either by the heathen themselves or by the chariots and litters on which they brought the exiles. Adam Clarke identifies one vehicle concretely: a pair of hampers or cradles thrown across a camel’s back, one on each side, each carrying a person and covered against rain and sun; he cites travellers who describe them, one reporting that at Aleppo women of inferior condition were on longer journeys stowed one on each side of a mule in a covered cradle. John Wesley reads the brethren as the children of Abraham considered as father of many nations and of the faithful, coming with as much joy and sincerity as the godly Jews bring their offerings in clean vessels. John Gill takes the whole of the Gentiles rather than the Jews, the bringing in of their fulness by those who escape the calamities of that time, and calls the Gentiles the brethren of converted Jews since all the Lord’s people are in a spiritual sense the children of Abraham.

The promise about priests raises the chapter’s sharpest question of scope. Ellicott states it plainly: we must determine whether Gentile converts are to be enrolled among the priests and Levites, or Israelites of the non-priestly tribes. Was the prophet breaking down the middle wall of partition, or clinging to it? An earlier verse favours the latter, he thinks, and he takes the thought to be that all Israel should be eligible for the priesthood—though capable of expansion to the whole Israel of God. Keil and Delitzsch argue the other way. Two scholars refer the phrase to the Israelites brought home, but then something would be promised which needed no promise, since the right of the native priest was not neutralised by sojourn abroad. Gill takes it of the Gentiles and limits it further: not the spiritual priesthood common to all believers, since only some of those brought are taken for priests, but the ministers of the word, called priests in Old Testament language though never so called in the New. Wesley agrees that God will find among the converted Gentiles those who, though not of the priestly tribe, do the true work of priests. Clarke notes that fifty-nine manuscripts and all the ancient versions add a conjunction the sense seems to require.

The permanence promised at the end is measured against the new creation. Keil and Delitzsch state the contrast: the great mass of the nations and of Israel perish, but the seed and name of Israel continue for ever like the new heaven and new earth; and because Israel’s calling towards the nations is fulfilled, the old fencing off of Israel ends and the qualification for priestly office is no longer descent but inward nobility. Ellicott says the future kingdom perpetuates the historical continuity of what preceded it, so that Israel shall still exist and the ideal represented by that name will have indestructible vitality, though he thinks the prophet’s vision limited to the outward Israel where the Apostle extends it to the spiritual. Gill weighs whether the new heavens are those made at the beginning, the new state under the gospel, or literally new heavens made when the present ones perish, and prefers the last as avoiding an illustration of a thing by itself. Wesley takes them of the new state of the church under the Messiah, and reads the promise as one of a daily succession of believers for its upholding.
23:
The last two verses close the book, and are read as a deliberate pair. Charles Ellicott notes that as at the close of two earlier sections, so here the vision of restoration is balanced by that of the righteous condemnation of the wicked. On the worship promised he observes that under the law Israelites were bound, at least in theory, to attend the temple at the three great feasts, whereas in the new Jerusalem the pilgrimages would be both more frequent and more universal, every sabbath and new moon witnessing not Israel only but all flesh thronging into the courts. The words, he adds, never have received and never can receive a literal fulfilment, their true realisation being found in the new Jerusalem of the Revelation and in the perpetual sabbath-keeping of the Epistle. Keil and Delitzsch take the promise literally: new moons and sabbaths will still be celebrated, the difference being that where all Israel once assembled at the three great feasts, now all flesh journeys to Jerusalem every new moon and sabbath. They parse the recurring phrase closely, taking the noun in the sense of what is due or fitting, so that the clause means as often as what befits the new moon occurs. John Wesley declines both extremes: there shall be in the gospel church as settled a course of worship, though of another nature, as ever there was in the Jewish, since Christians are not bound to keep the Jewish sabbaths but New Testament worship is expressed in Old Testament phrases; where the Jews appeared three times a year, the gospel church shall worship from one sabbath to another. John Gill attends only to the rendering, that the phrase runs from month in its months.

The final verse is the hardest in the book to place: does it speak of this world or the next? Ellicott argues that the imagery is suggested by the great battle described earlier, those slain in it filling the valleys round Jerusalem, devoured by worms or given to the flames; taken strictly, the words do not speak of the punishment of souls after death but of the destruction on earth of the enemies of God. The clauses about the undying worm and the unquenched fire, however, point to something more, to be read between the lines; and they became the starting-point of later Jewish thought about Gehenna, of the words in which our Lord gave utterance to what at least seemed to express those thoughts, and of the dominant eschatology of Christendom. Keil and Delitzsch keep the scene at Jerusalem: those who go up every new moon and sabbath see the punishment of the rebellious, and the neighbourhood becomes such a scene of judgment because the prophet had predicted that the whole multitude of its enemies would be crowded against it; the verb, they note, denotes a fixed and lingering look. Adam Clarke supplies the topography. The valley south-east of Jerusalem was where the idolatrous made their children pass through the fire; to stop the practice a king defiled it with bones, after which the carcasses of animals were thrown there and it became the common burying place for the poor. Our Saviour, Clarke says, expressed the state of the blessed by sensible images such as paradise or a place at table in the kingdom of heaven, since we could have no conception of it otherwise, and in the same way expressed the place of torment under the image of that valley, the worm preying on the carcasses and the fire consuming the victims—marking the difference that in the valley the suffering is transient and the worm itself dies. Gill takes the going forth not of leaving the city literally, as two Jewish commentators do, nor of rising from the grave, but of going out from the assemblies of the saints when fire comes down and destroys the wicked.
